We were spoken to by the only white man in San Crispobal de las casas, who seemed like CIA, asking us point blank what we were doing there, in a cafe. What are you going to do? Who are you going with? When are you leaving?

It felt important! 😂

In 2005, a few college friends and I visited Oventik, one of the Zapatista caracoles in Chiapas. We nearly died several times getting there. The mountain road wrapped around cliffs, and our rental car was barely running, which is a great combination when you're on your way to visit a revolution.

In San Cristóbal de las Casas, the only white man we met sat us down in a café and asked us questions so directly that he seemed like a CIA agent. Why were we there? Who did we work with? What were our plans? When were we leaving?

It made us feel important for a minute. We were college kids in a dying rental car, but apparently the empire had questions. 😂

The second thing I like is the principle of “mandar obedeciendo”, or leading by obeying. Their representatives must do what the assembly has decided and they are answerable to the people.

Thirdly, the zapatistas are the closest I’ve seen to an example of the whole thing being done. As well as their system of decision making they have set up their own systems of education, health, justice, production, political formation, how to teach people outside their communities and how to coordinate between communities.
community-s9b.u2-emuB:
Their main difference to other systems is how the representatives work; that is based on the principle of “mandar obedeciendo,” leading by obeying; that means that the representatives do what the assembly told them to do and are responsible to the people.

Another positive thing of the Zapatistas is that they are the most whole example that I have seen till now on how to build autonomy; they have their own education, health care, justice, collective production, political formation and are educating in different ways and have also coordination.
community-s9b.u2:
What impressed me most was how they handle authority. They call it mandar obedeciendo, leading by obeying. Representatives carry out what the assembly decided, and they stay answerable to the people who gave them the mandate.

The Zapatistas are also the closest thing to a whole example that I found, because for them autonomy is more than a way of voting. They've built their own education and health care. They run their own justice, collective production and political formation, and they've worked out ways of teaching outsiders. And they coordinate beyond a single village.
community-s9b.u3-emuA:
In 2023, after a long internal review process, the Zapatistas decreed the dissolution of their level of regional government, the so-called Rebel Zapatista Autonomous Municipalities and Good Government Juntas. They now operate through a network of Local Autonomous Governments which, if they so choose, can form regional coordinating collectives, but which are not above the Local Autonomous Governments.

While most institutions tend to accumulate bureaucratic levels and offices as they age, the Zapatistas reviewed their own institutions and, rather than writing a book on leadership and setting up some kind of certification, modified their own system.
community-s9b.u3-emuB:
One of the many interesting decisions made by the zapatistas in 2023, after a long internal review process, was the decision to dissolve the “Rebel Zapatista Autonomous Municipalities” and “Good Government Juntas”, and to pass the authority to new “Local Autonomous Governments” in each community, which can still form regional collectives to coordinate, but which won’t be above the Local Autonomous Governments, but under them.

While most institutions tend to accumulate more and more instances and offices over time, the zapatistas decided to go through a review process and move the authority down. And the interesting thing is that they didn’t publish a book on leadership and start a certification program, but they changed their own system!
community-s9b.u3:
In 2023, after a long internal review, the Zapatistas announced they were dissolving the Rebel Zapatista Autonomous Municipalities and the Good Government Juntas. Under their new arrangement, authority moved toward Local Autonomous Governments in each community. Those local governments can coordinate through regional collectives, but the coordinating levels are explicitly described as dependent on the communities. They don't sit above them.

Most institutions pile up layers and offices as they get older. The Zapatistas reviewed theirs and pushed authority down. They didn't put out a leadership book and start a certification program. They changed the system they were actually living in.

Sorry for the enthusiasm! I have to restrain myself. This may be a way to proceed for the Zapatistas, with their very long history and all the different things they share, but this will be a very long process for a new ecovillage, and there is no way that the trust that is necessary to make it work can be achieved in a short time. What I mean is that the diagram can’t be copied.

The Zapatistas have said before that Zapatismo can’t be imported or exported. The diagram is not the interesting part. What’s interesting is that they are learning and modifying the structure as it is built.
community-s9b.u4-emuB:
In this case, I need to moderate my enthusiasm. I’m aware that it takes a long time to build something like the Zapatistas’ form of autonomy. They are Indigenous people, with a long history, who share a struggle over land, language, kinship, etc. It will take a long time to build this kind of trust in a new ecovillage, and trying to immitate the visible aspect (the diagram) won’t get people there.

By the way, the Zapatistas themselves have said many times that Zapatismo is neither importable nor exportable. It’s not the diagram that is useful, but the way they learn and change their structures.
community-s9b.u4:
I need to restrain my enthusiasm here, though. Zapatista autonomy grew out of Indigenous communities with long histories, who share land struggles, language and kinship, and have defended themselves together for decades. A new ecovillage can't copy the visible diagram and get the trust underneath it right away.

The Zapatistas themselves have warned people against importing or exporting Zapatismo as a ready-made model. Their diagram isn't the useful part. The useful part is how they learn: they build, ask, find out where the practice fails, and change the structure.
community-s9b.u5-emuA: Sorry, I meant to add that it doesn't prove the entirety of the model I put forth as the end state of a post money economy, which would also include removing the need for "outside" money, as it moves away from the common purse and developing internal necessities without the use of pricing and money. The Zapatistas still do sell and trade, and do receive support from the outside, but they do provide the main necessities and functions of their society, such as schools, clinics, the apparatus of their government, and most of their resistance through collective work. Just something to be aware of, since support from the outside can often end up creating gate keepers and negative dependencies.
community-s9b.u5-emuB: Also, that doesn't mean I'm saying that's how the whole economy should work, it's just one step along the way. I mean even the Zapatistas work together collectively to fund their schools, clinics, government, resistance, etc., but they also have to sell products and trade and get help from outside their communities in order to survive. Which is a good thing up to a point, as it can lead to dependency and the rise of gatekeepers.
community-s9b.u5: They also don't prove my whole economic path, from unpriced internal necessities to a common purse to eliminating outside money. Zapatista communities use collective work to support their schools, clinics, autonomous government and resistance. They also sell products, trade, and receive outside support. What they show is that major necessities and public functions can be taken out of ordinary market purchase and governed collectively. Outside help can build capability. But it can also create gatekeepers and uneven dependence, when the specialist, donor or organization stays indispensable.
community-s9b.u6-emuA:
To celebrate the tenth anniversary of their autonomous governments, some Zapatista communities opened an Escuelita, inviting outsiders to live with families and learn about their form of autonomy through participating in it. Around a thousand and a half people came for the first round of Escuelitas, and thousands more for subsequent ones.

One of the ways an escuelita can fail is to turn the community into a kind of business that is based on hosting outsiders. Then the whole life of the community is geared towards putting on a show for outsiders to watch. The success of the escuelita is measured not by how many daughter communities are created, but by how many people come to visit. It becomes about giving people a transformative experience for a week, rather than teaching them the social and material details of how the community’s system works, so that they can set up something similar elsewhere.
community-s9b.u6-emuB:
One of the things the Zapatistas did to celebrate the tenth anniversary of their creation of autonomous governments was to open “Escuelita”, inviting outsiders to come live with families and learn about what autonomy is like by participating in it. About a thousand and a half people came for the first couple, and thousands for subsequent ones.

There are several ways this kind of thing, an escuelita, can go wrong. The worst is when the village or community turns it into a business, and reorients its life to “put on a show” for outsiders. Then the number of “daughter communities” they create is measured in the number of people they can convince to spend a week with them and say they were changed by the experience, rather than the number of people who learned enough about the social and material system to recreate it in a new place.
community-s9b.u6:
For the tenth anniversary of their autonomous governments, the Zapatistas opened the Escuelita. Outsiders lived with families and learned autonomy by taking part in their daily life. Around 1,500 students came to the first sessions, and thousands more came to later ones.

An escuelita can fail by turning into a visitor business, where residents spend their lives performing community for paying outsiders, and the number of guests replaces the number of daughter communities as the measure of success. Making people feel transformed for a week isn't the point. The point is to teach enough of the social and material system that some of them can build it somewhere else.
community-s9b.u7-emuA:
In my research I have looked for information about what came out of the Escuelita and I am impressed by what I see (alumni, people taking things home, organizing, etc). But I am not aware of seeing any evidence of a linear connection between someone attending the Escuelita and then setting up communal institutions and seeing how those institutions and their kids did. And the Zapatistas were influencing people internationally before the Escuelita even existed. So I don’t feel that I am taking something that was proven by the Zapatistas, so much as taking their approach to teaching and trying to replicate that.

Sociocracy has some similar form factors, but they come from a very different history. They are great for people building things to look into though.
community-s9b.u7-emuB:
I’ve been doing a little research to see how the Escuelita was effective at spreading the good word. It seems that a lot of good things have happened as a result of the Escuelita, but I haven’t found any direct links from someone attending the Escuelita and then setting up similar institutions in their own communities, with data on how those institutions and their children have fared. It’s also hard to separate the effect of the Escuelita from the effect of the Zapatista movement in general (the international influence preceded the creation of the Escuelita). So I’m borrowing their basic approach to teaching and their desire to replicate, but not citing them as evidence that the approach works.

It’s interesting to see that a movement with a completely different history, namely Sociocracy , has developed a lot of the same form.
community-s9b.u7:
In my research, I also tried to trace what happened after the Escuelita. I found alumni networks, people bringing practices home, and later organizing. But I didn't find a clean line from an Escuelita student to a newly founded communal institution, with evidence of how that institution's members and their children actually did over time. Zapatista influence was already spreading internationally before the Escuelita, so a later resemblance doesn't prove it came from there. What I'm borrowing is a way of teaching and the ambition to replicate. I'm not claiming the Zapatistas already proved my whole model.

Sociocracy arrives at some similar forms from a very different history, with its circles, consent, distributed authority and links between levels. The resemblance doesn't prove there's a universal formula. But it gives builders another serious system to study, so they don't have to invent their governance in the middle of their first dispute.
